subsection: 2. The structures of European diplomacy, the New Imperialism and colonial rivalries, 1890–1914

notes.h: Bismarck's system and why it ended: the Reinsurance Treaty lapses
notes.b: To follow the alliances after 1890 you need to know what they replaced. Bismarck had built a web of agreements to keep France isolated, and his successors let part of it drop, which opened the way for new groupings.
points: French hostility to Germany after Germany annexed Alsace-Lorraine in 1871 (the wish for revenge, called revanche) was the fixed point of European diplomacy, so Bismarck's aim was to keep France without allies.

Bismarck's alliances were the Dual Alliance of 1879 (Germany and Austria-Hungary), the Triple Alliance of 1882 (with Italy added) and the secret Reinsurance Treaty of 1887 (Germany and Russia, for three years). Together they kept France isolated and avoided a war on two fronts.
Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in March 1890 and began a 'new course' in foreign policy. Leo von Caprivi became Chancellor (1890-94).

In 1890 Caprivi and Friedrich von Holstein (a senior Foreign Office official) let the Reinsurance Treaty lapse. They thought it inconsistent with the Dual Alliance and harmful to relations with Britain.
Letting the treaty go left Russia with no German link and no friends, which is why it looked elsewhere. This was the first step in the break-up of Bismarck's balance of power.
notes.tip: Exams ask how Europe split into two blocs after 1890. Start from the lapse of the Reinsurance Treaty in 1890, with Caprivi and Holstein and their reasons, because it explains why Russia and France moved together.

notes.b: Russia, left without a German partner, and France, still isolated since 1871, had a shared interest in finding a friend. Their agreement ended France's isolation and was a real military alliance, unlike the later ententes.
points: French banks began making large loans to Russia from 1888, which gave the two countries a financial link before any political one.
A French naval squadron visited Kronstadt (Russia's naval base) in July 1891, and in August 1891 the two powers agreed a political understanding to consult each other if war threatened.

A military convention was signed in August 1892 and ratified by an exchange of letters completed in January 1894. It was secret and defensive, aimed at the Triple Alliance powers, so each ally was protected without attacking anyone.

Its terms: if France was attacked by Germany, or by Italy supported by Germany, Russia would attack Germany; if Russia was attacked by Germany, or by Austria-Hungary supported by Germany, France would attack Germany.
Both would also mobilise (call up their armies) if any Triple Alliance power mobilised, which meant a crisis involving one Triple Alliance member could draw in both allies.

Because of this, Germany now faced the danger of a war on two fronts, the very risk Bismarck had worked to avoid, and this later shaped the Schlieffen Plan (Germany's war plan against France and Russia).
French investment in Russian railways and industry cemented the alliance. It lasted until the Russian revolution and Russia's exit from the war in 1917-18.
notes.tip: Learn the dates and terms: military convention 1892, ratified January 1894, defensive, with mobilisation if any Triple Alliance power mobilised. Do not mix it up with the Entente Cordiale or Anglo-Russian Entente, which were colonial settlements, not alliances.

notes.h: Britain leaves splendid isolation: Japan and the Entente Cordiale
notes.b: Britain had long avoided permanent peacetime alliances, a policy called 'splendid isolation'. By 1900 that policy was costing it more than it gave, so Britain began to settle quarrels with its imperial rivals and to find partners.
points: Isolation lost its value because European opinion was hostile to Britain during the Boer War, and because Germany was starting to build a large navy that threatened British sea power. Joseph Chamberlain, the Colonial Secretary, sought an alliance with Germany in 1898-1901, but the talks failed.
The Anglo-Japanese Alliance (1902) gave Britain support in the Far East against Russia, so it could keep more of its navy nearer home. It was renewed in 1905 and 1911.
Théophile Delcassé, French foreign minister 1898-1905, was the French architect of an agreement with Britain, and Edward VII's visit to Paris in May 1903 helped warm opinion.

The Entente Cordiale was signed on 8 April 1904 by Lord Lansdowne (British Foreign Secretary) and Paul Cambon (French ambassador in London). France accepted Britain's position in Egypt and Britain accepted France's in Morocco.
It also settled disputes over the Newfoundland fisheries, West Africa, Siam, Madagascar and the New Hebrides, so it removed the colonial quarrels that had made the two powers rivals.

The Entente was not an alliance, because neither promised to fight for the other. It tightened over time: secret Anglo-French military staff talks began in 1906, and in 1912 a naval arrangement concentrated the French fleet in the Mediterranean and the British fleet in the North Sea and Channel.
notes.tip: Examiners expect you to say why Britain gave up isolation: European hostility during the Boer War, German naval building and the failure of the Chamberlain talks. Call the 1904 Entente a colonial settlement, not an alliance, and keep Delcassé (foreign minister) apart from Cambon (ambassador who signed).

notes.h: The Anglo-Russian Entente and the two blocs
notes.b: Britain's quarrels with Russia in Asia were the last big obstacle to a grouping against Germany. Settling them completed the Triple Entente, which stood opposite the older Triple Alliance.
points: Russia had been weakened by defeat by Japan in 1904-05 and both Russia and Britain were worried about Germany, which is why they were ready to compromise.
The Anglo-Russian Convention (31 August 1907) was agreed by Sir Edward Grey (Foreign Secretary) and Alexander Izvolsky (Russian foreign minister).
Its terms: Persia was divided into a Russian zone in the north, a British zone in the south-east and a neutral zone between. Afghanistan was a British sphere, and both promised to keep out of Tibet.

The Triple Entente of Britain, France and Russia was therefore a loose understanding with no common military commitment. It faced the formal Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy, which had been renewed in 1887, 1891, 1902 and, for the last time, 1912.

The Triple Alliance was weaker than it looked because Italy was unreliable. In 1902 the Prinetti-Barrere agreement secretly promised France that Italy would stay neutral if France was attacked, and in 1911-12 Italy fought the Ottoman Empire for Libya.

From about 1905 the blocs hardened. Germany spoke of 'encirclement' (being surrounded by hostile powers), while Britain and France feared German ambitions, so each crisis looked like a test of strength between the blocs.
In short, the balance of power had changed from Bismarck's flexible system, built around Germany, to two armed camps.
notes.tip: Students often call the Triple Entente an alliance and swap it with the Triple Alliance. Remember: Entente is Britain, France and Russia and was loose; Alliance is Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy and was formal.

notes.h: What the New Imperialism was and the economic motives
notes.b: From about 1880 to 1914 European states rushed to take colonies and spheres of influence (areas where one power claimed special rights). Historians call this the New Imperialism and ask first what economic motives drove it.
points: It differed from earlier empire-building in its speed, its scale, the number of powers taking part, and its targets, mainly Africa and China. It also spread beyond Europe, to the USA and Japan.

The second industrial revolution (the spread of industry using steel, electricity and chemicals) created demand for raw materials and markets, which is why industrial states looked overseas. One clause is enough here: the detail is in the notes on German industrialisation.
Industrial states needed raw materials such as rubber, cotton, palm oil, copper, gold and diamonds, and later oil.
They also wanted protected markets, because tariffs rose in Europe from the late 1870s, and outlets for investment overseas.

The British economist J.A. Hobson, who reported on the Boer War for the Manchester Guardian, argued in Imperialism: A Study (1902) that surplus capital and underconsumption (too little buying power) at home drove capitalists to invest overseas and so drove empire.
Lenin, in Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (written 1916, published 1917), called imperialism the last stage of capitalism, leading to war between capitalist states.
Historians dispute the theory. Germany's colonies took a tiny share of its trade and investment, and much British investment went to the USA and Latin America, outside the empire.
notes.tip: Do not state that most trade and investment went outside the empires as a general rule. It is true of Germany and much British investment, so use those cases. Keep Hobson (British liberal economist, 1902) apart from Lenin (Marxist, written 1916).

notes.h: Strategic, nationalist, missionary and ideological motives, and what made conquest possible
notes.b: Profit was only one reason, and for many states not the main one. Strategy, prestige, religion and ideas of racial superiority also pushed governments and public opinion towards empire, and new technology made it practical.
points: Strategic: states sought naval bases, coaling stations and secure routes. Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 to protect the Suez Canal (opened 1869), the route to India, and then moved to control the Nile valley to keep that route safe.

Nationalist: colonies were seen as a mark of Great Power status, and the popular press, colonial societies and public opinion cheered each acquisition. After defeat in 1871 France sought compensation overseas under Jules Ferry (Prime Minister 1880-81 and 1883-85), who promoted expansion in Tunisia (1881) and Indochina (Tonkin).

Missionary and humanitarian: churches wanted to spread Christianity and end the slave trade. The Scottish missionary David Livingstone (died 1873) and the explorer H.M. Stanley, who found him in 1871, made Africa known to the public.

Ideological: Social Darwinism applied the phrase 'survival of the fittest', coined by Herbert Spencer (1864), to nations and races, so rule over others was justified as natural. Related was a belief in a duty to 'civilise' other peoples, France's mission civilisatrice.
Kipling's poem 'The White Man's Burden' (1899), written about the USA in the Philippines, expressed this duty to civilise.

Technology made conquest possible: quinine against malaria, steamships, railways, the telegraph and breech-loading rifles, and the Maxim gun (the first fully automatic machine gun, invented by Hiram Maxim in 1884) gave Europeans an overwhelming military advantage.
Competition fed on itself, which is why even poor land was claimed. Once one power claimed territory, others annexed land before they could be shut out, even where the land was of little value.
notes.tip: For why powers sought colonies, give a range of motives (economic, strategic, nationalist, missionary, ideological), each with a named example, add technology and the point that rivalry fed on itself, and then weigh them: prestige and strategy mattered more than profit for many states because colonies often did not pay.

notes.h: The Scramble for Africa and the Berlin Conference
notes.b: Africa was the main prize of the New Imperialism. In about thirty years almost the whole continent was divided, and a conference in Berlin gave the process its rules.
points: In 1880 only about a tenth of Africa was under European control, mostly coastal areas such as Algeria, the Cape and Senegal; by 1914 about nine tenths of the continent had been taken (textbook estimates).
The scramble was triggered by Leopold II's claims on the Congo, France's advance in West Africa and its protectorate over Tunisia (1881), and Britain's occupation of Egypt in 1882.

The Berlin Conference (15 November 1884 to 26 February 1885) was called by Bismarck with French agreement. Fourteen states attended, including the USA and the Ottoman Empire. Do not confuse it with the Congress of Berlin of 1878, which dealt with the Balkans.

Its General Act required powers to notify each other of claims and to show effective occupation (real control, at first of coasts), and declared free trade in the Congo basin and free navigation on the Congo and Niger rivers.
During the conference the powers recognised the claim of Leopold's association to the Congo; the Congo Free State was proclaimed afterwards, in 1885.

No African ruler took part. The Conference did not itself divide Africa, but it made the partition faster and gave it a legal shape, because anyone could now claim land by occupying it and giving notice.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions on the Scramble reward the extent by 1914, the Berlin Conference rules, the main colonies of named powers, and Fashoda or the Congo. Accurate dates and named examples earn the marks.

notes.h: Rival plans and the partition of Africa
notes.b: Once the rules were set, the powers had competing plans. Where plans crossed they risked war, and where they could, they traded claims by agreement.
points: Britain's aim was a belt of territory from the Cape to Cairo under British rule. Its leading backer was Cecil Rhodes, a mining magnate (diamonds and gold) who founded the British South Africa Company in 1889 and was Prime Minister of the Cape Colony 1890-96; Rhodesia was named after him.
France sought an east-west belt linking its West African lands with Djibouti on the Red Sea. The two plans crossed at Fashoda in 1898.
Germany, a latecomer, took South West Africa, Togo, Cameroon and German East Africa (1884-85). Italy took Eritrea and Italian Somaliland and, in 1911-12, Libya. Portugal held Angola and Mozambique.
Disputes were often settled by compromise. In the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty (1 July 1890) Britain gave Germany the North Sea island of Heligoland and Germany recognised British control of Zanzibar.
Africans resisted, for example Ethiopia, under Emperor Menelik II, defeated Italy at the Battle of Adwa (1 March 1896), which kept it independent.
By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia were independent African states.

notes.h: Leopold II and the Congo Free State
notes.b: The Congo shows the New Imperialism at its worst. Its ruler was a king acting as a private owner, and the system he set up brought a public scandal that forced change.
points: Leopold II, King of the Belgians 1865-1909, founded the International African Association in 1876, and Stanley worked for him in the Congo from 1879.
The Congo Free State was proclaimed in 1885 as Leopold's personal state, not a Belgian colony, on promises to end slavery and keep free trade.
From the 1890s Africans were forced to collect wild rubber under quotas, because demand for bicycle and later motor-car tyres made it very profitable. This is known as the 'red rubber' system.
Failure to meet quotas was punished by taking women as hostages, flogging with the chicotte (a whip), cutting off hands, and burning villages.

The Force Publique, the colonial army of African soldiers under European officers, enforced the system. The population fell by millions from violence, disease, flight and famine, because the system destroyed villages and food supplies, but estimates vary widely.

E.D. Morel, a shipping-company clerk in Liverpool, noticed that ships brought rubber and ivory from the Congo but carried back mostly guns and ammunition. This suggested forced labour, and he campaigned on it.
Roger Casement, an Irish-born British consul, wrote a report on the Congo published in 1904. Morel, with Casement, founded the Congo Reform Association in 1904.

Writers helped the campaign: Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness (1899) drew on his own Congo journey of 1890, and Mark Twain wrote King Leopold's Soliloquy (1905). Under international pressure Belgium annexed the colony in 1908 as the Belgian Congo, and Leopold died in 1909.
notes.tip: Give no Congo death toll, because estimates vary widely. Keep Morel (journalist and campaigner) apart from Casement (consul who wrote the report), and Leopold's Free State (personal, to 1908) apart from the Belgian Congo (state colony from 1908). Note the significance: the first international humanitarian campaign against a colonial regime.

notes.h: Imperial rivalry in Asia and the Pacific
notes.b: In Asia the powers competed less for conquest than for ports, trade and influence, and China was the main target because it was too weak to resist. Two newer powers, the USA and Japan, joined in.
points: In South-East Asia France formed French Indochina in 1887 (Vietnam and Cambodia, with Laos added in 1893). Britain annexed Upper Burma in 1886 and extended control over Malaya; the Dutch held the East Indies.
Japan defeated China in the Sino-Japanese War (1894-95) and won Taiwan (Formosa). In the Triple Intervention of 1895 Russia, France and Germany forced Japan to give back the Liaodong peninsula.

The powers then scrambled for concessions (1897-98). Germany seized Kiaochow (Jiaozhou) in 1897 after two German missionaries were killed, and leased it in 1898; Russia leased Port Arthur, Britain Weihaiwei and France Guangzhouwan (1898-99).
Each claimed a sphere of influence: Russia in Manchuria, Germany in Shandong, Britain in the Yangtze valley and France in the south.

The USA defeated Spain in the Spanish-American War (1898) and took the Philippines, Guam and Puerto Rico. In 1899 its Secretary of State, John Hay, sent the Open Door notes asking for equal trading rights for all in China.

The Boxer Rising (1899-1901) was a Chinese uprising against foreigners and Christians. The foreign legations (embassies) in Beijing were besieged from June to August 1900 and relieved by an eight-nation force of Britain, France, Germany, Russia, Japan, the USA, Italy and Austria-Hungary.

Japan began to modernise after the Meiji Restoration of 1868, building a strong army and navy. It defeated Russia in the Russo-Japanese War (1904-05, ended by the Treaty of Portsmouth), the first time an Asian power beat a European Great Power in modern times.

The defeat turned Russia's attention back to the Balkans and Europe, contributed to the revolution of 1905, and opened the way to the 1907 Entente with Britain. The course of the war belongs to the notes on Tsarist Russia.
notes.tip: Keep the two Japanese wars apart: the Sino-Japanese War (1894-95) was Japan beating China, and the Russo-Japanese War (1904-05) was Japan beating Russia. Kiaochow is needed in one clause only.

notes.b: Fashoda was the sharpest colonial clash between two European powers in this period. It nearly caused war between Britain and France, but it ended in a settlement that led towards friendship.
points: Britain had occupied Egypt in 1882 and treated the whole Nile valley as its sphere, while France wanted an east-west belt across Africa, so the two plans collided on the Upper Nile.
In July 1898 Captain Jean-Baptiste Marchand's small French expedition reached Fashoda on the Upper Nile in Sudan.
Kitchener defeated the Mahdist army at Omdurman on 2 September 1898, then reached Fashoda in September with a much larger force. Both sides refused to withdraw and war was feared.
France agreed to withdraw in November 1898. Delcassé judged that France could not risk war with Britain's navy; France was isolated and facing the Dreyfus Affair at home.
An Anglo-French agreement of March 1899 set the boundary between the two spheres: the Nile valley British and the area west of it French.
Fashoda was the worst Anglo-French crisis of the period, but it showed the danger of colonial clashes and convinced both sides to settle disputes, which led to the 1904 Entente Cordiale.
notes.tip: Fashoda was Britain against France in Sudan and did not involve Germany, so do not treat it as a Moroccan crisis. Remember Kitchener is the same man at Omdurman, Fashoda and, later, in the Boer War.

notes.b: Britain's war against the Boer republics was a colonial war that damaged Britain's reputation in Europe. It exposed how few friends Britain had, which helped push it out of isolation.
points: The Boer republics were the Transvaal (South African Republic, under President Paul Kruger) and the Orange Free State. Gold found on the Witwatersrand in 1886 drew in Uitlanders (foreign, mostly British, settlers in the Transvaal, who were denied the vote), and this led to disputes with Britain.

The failed Jameson Raid (December 1895 to January 1896), an armed incursion into the Transvaal led by Rhodes's associate Leander Starr Jameson, soured relations, and Rhodes resigned as Cape Prime Minister. Wilhelm II's Kruger telegram of January 1896, congratulating Kruger, caused outrage in Britain.
The war began on 11 October 1899. The Boers won early successes, including Black Week in December 1899 (three British defeats) and sieges of Ladysmith, Kimberley and Mafeking.
Britain sent large reinforcements under Lord Roberts, and from late 1900 under Kitchener. Mafeking was relieved in May 1900, and the Boers turned to guerrilla war (small raids and ambushes).

From 1900, and especially under Kitchener, the British burned Boer farms and moved Boer civilians into concentration camps. Over 20,000 Boer civilians died in them, most of them children. Black Africans were held in separate camps where many thousands died (figures uncertain).
Emily Hobhouse exposed the camps. The Treaty of Vereeniging (31 May 1902) made the Transvaal and Orange Free State British colonies.

The war showed Britain's isolation and aroused hostility in Europe, damaged British prestige and military reputation, and pushed Britain to end splendid isolation. Hobson's critique of imperialism arose from it.
At home it fed popular excitement: when Mafeking was relieved in May 1900 there were wild celebrations in London (Mafeking night).
notes.tip: Do not write that Kitchener burned farms and interned civilians from the start: it began under Roberts in 1900 and expanded under Kitchener. Give only 'over 20,000 Boer civilians' for camp deaths, and no figure for black African deaths. Keep Rhodes (Cape politician) apart from Jameson (who led the raid).

notes.h: The first Moroccan crisis: Tangier and Algeciras (1905-06)
notes.b: Morocco was one of the last independent states in Africa. When France moved to control it, Germany tried to test the new Entente, and the result was the opposite of what Germany wanted.
points: The 1904 Entente gave France a free hand in Morocco. Germany aimed to test or break the Entente, to win compensation, and to assert its say in colonial questions.
Wilhelm II landed at Tangier on 31 March 1905 and declared support for the Sultan's independence. This was a challenge to France.
German pressure forced Delcassé to resign in June 1905.
The crisis ended at the Algeciras Conference (January to April 1906). France and Spain were given the policing of Morocco's ports, and France's influence over Morocco's finances was recognised.
It was a diplomatic defeat for Germany, because Germany was supported only by Austria-Hungary, while Britain and Russia backed France.
The crisis strengthened the Entente: British and French generals began secret staff talks in 1906, so a colonial settlement became closer to a quasi-alliance.
notes.tip: Do not say the United States backed France at Algeciras. Say Germany was supported only by Austria-Hungary and that Britain and Russia backed France. Keep Tangier (Wilhelm's 1905 landing) and Algeciras (the 1906 conference) apart from Agadir (1911).

notes.b: Five years later France tightened its hold on Morocco and Germany challenged it again. This time Britain's warning showed how closely it now stood by France.
points: In May 1911 French troops entered Fez. Alfred von Kiderlen-Wachter, the German foreign secretary, directed German policy.
The German gunboat Panther arrived at Agadir on 1 July 1911. Germany demanded compensation.
David Lloyd George, Chancellor of the Exchequer, gave the Mansion House speech on 21 July 1911, warning Germany that Britain would not be pushed aside.

The crisis was settled by a Franco-German agreement on 4 November 1911: Germany accepted French control of Morocco in return for a strip of the French Congo added to Cameroon. The Treaty of Fez (30 March 1912) made Morocco a French protectorate.
Many Germans saw the settlement as a humiliation because Germany had gained only a strip of the Congo. It drew Britain and France closer, and the Anglo-French naval arrangement followed in 1912.
Italy seized the moment, for example, to attack the Ottoman Empire in September 1911.
notes.tip: Say Agadir drew Britain and France closer and that the 1912 naval arrangement followed, not that it was the only cause. For each crisis (Fashoda, Boer War, Tangier and Algeciras, Agadir) know one cause, the events in order, the outcome and one effect on alliances.

notes.b: Colonial rivalry did not stay overseas. It shaped relations between the Great Powers, the mood of public opinion and even the way governments counted the cost of empire.
points: Imperial rivalry produced crises that raised tension and caused war scares between Great Powers: Fashoda, the Boer War and Morocco.
It was also settled by compromise: Heligoland-Zanzibar (1890), Fashoda (1899), and the agreements of 1904 and 1907. These colonial settlements became the basis of the ententes.

It changed the balance of power, so alignments shifted. Britain moved from isolation into the Entente, and Germany's clumsy colonial diplomacy, such as its challenges in Morocco, left it more isolated.
It fed nationalism, jingoism (aggressive patriotism) and militarism at home, through the popular press, celebrations such as Mafeking night (1900), and demands for bigger navies and armies.
Economic effects were mixed. Colonies supplied raw materials and returns on investment, but they often cost more than they earned: Germany's colonies took a tiny share of its trade.
Humanitarian opinion reacted. The Congo and Boer-camp scandals showed that public opinion could expose and restrain abuses.
notes.tip: Effects answers need Europe and international relations, not only colonised peoples: crises, Britain's realignment, hardening blocs, jingoism and militarism, and compromise settlements.

notes.h: Assessment: did imperial rivalry cause tension in Europe?
notes.b: Examiners want a judgement with both sides. Colonial quarrels created friction, but they were mostly resolved, so the question is how much they mattered beside Europe's own rivalries.
points: For tension: imperial rivalry created crises (Fashoda, the Boer War and Morocco) that raised tension and made Britain and Germany suspicious of each other.
Against: imperial agreements also reduced tension, as the Entente Cordiale and the Anglo-Russian Entente show; the powers were often able to settle colonial quarrels by compromise.
For: the Moroccan crises hardened the blocs, turning the Entente Cordiale from a colonial settlement into a quasi-alliance.
Against: colonial disputes were mostly settled peacefully, so war in 1914 came from the Balkans and Europe's own alliance system rather than from colonial clashes.
Contemporaries differed: Germans blamed British and French encirclement for their insecurity, while the British and French blamed German pressure for the Moroccan crises.

Hobson and Lenin, writing from different positions, saw capitalism and imperialism as an underlying cause of war. Later historians see imperialism as one factor alongside alliances, militarism and nationalism.
On the alliance system, it helped keep the balance of power and deter war by making each side cautious, but it also tied powers to each other, so that a local crisis could become a general war.
notes.tip: For 'to what extent' questions, give both sides and a judgement. Morocco is the best case for imperialism hardening the blocs, while the fact that 1914 began in the Balkans is the best case against. Imperial rivalry and the blocs are two strands among Franco-German hostility, Balkan rivalry and the naval race.

keyTerms.definition: The competition from about 1880 among European powers, and later the United States and Japan, to acquire colonies and spheres of influence in Africa, Asia and the Pacific.
A situation in which no one state can dominate Europe because rival states ally or act together to check it; the alliance blocs of 1890-1914 were meant to preserve it.
Pride in and loyalty to one's own nation, which made colonies a matter of prestige and strengthened rivalry between the powers.
The loose grouping of Britain, France and Russia, formed by the Franco-Russian Alliance (1894), Entente Cordiale (1904) and Anglo-Russian Entente (1907).
The 1904 agreement settling colonial disputes between Britain and France, giving Britain a free hand in Egypt and France in Morocco.
The application of the idea of the survival of the fittest to nations and races, used to justify conquest and the idea of a civilising mission.
The rapid European partition of Africa between about 1880 and 1914, which left only Ethiopia and Liberia independent.
The rule agreed at the Berlin Conference that a power had to administer and control territory, not merely claim it, for its claim to be recognised.
A region, such as parts of China or Persia, in which one power held special economic or political privileges without formal annexation.
Britain's policy of avoiding permanent alliances with other European powers, abandoned in the early 1900s.

factCards.definition: A military convention of 1892, ratified in January 1894; a defensive pact against the Triple Alliance powers.
8 April 1904; Britain recognised in Egypt, France in Morocco, with other colonial disputes settled.
31 August 1907; Persia divided into Russian, British and neutral zones, Afghanistan a British sphere, Tibet left alone.

factCards.term: Why did Italy weaken the Triple Alliance?
factCards.definition: In 1902 it secretly promised France neutrality, and in 1911-12 it fought the Ottomans for Libya.
Notice of claims, effective occupation, and free trade on the Congo and Niger; no Africans took part.

factCards.term: Scramble for Africa: how much was taken?
factCards.definition: About 10 percent under European control in 1880 and about 90 percent by 1914; only Ethiopia and Liberia stayed independent.

factCards.term: Leopold II and the Congo: the key facts
factCards.definition: The Congo Free State (recognised 1885) was his personal possession; forced rubber collection caused mass death; Belgium took over in 1908 after the campaign of Morel and Casement.
Ethiopia defeated an Italian army, preserving its independence.
Marchand's small French force faced Kitchener's larger British force; France withdrew in November 1898 and a boundary agreement followed in 1899.
1899-1902, ended by the Treaty of Vereeniging on 31 May 1902; Britain used concentration camps, in which over 20,000 Boer civilians died.
Wilhelm II's Tangier visit (31 March 1905) challenged France; Algeciras (1906) ended in a German diplomatic defeat.
Germany sent the Panther to Agadir in July; in November it accepted French control of Morocco in return for part of the French Congo.

factCards.term: Who wrote the main economic critiques of imperialism?
factCards.definition: J.A. Hobson (Imperialism: A Study, 1902) and Lenin (Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism, 1916).
A British alliance with Japan that ended Britain's isolation and was renewed in 1905 and 1911.
